parole.testo: From Old Danish -makæræ, from Old Norse -makari (“-maker”), from Middle Low German -maker

From Old Norse alvara, from an adjective ǫlværr (“benevolent”), maybe from Middle Low German alwār (“true, kind, benevolent”), cognate with German albern (“silly”), Old High German alawāri (“true, friendly”), a compound of Proto-Germanic *allaz, *ala- (“all”) and *wēraz, *wērijaz (“true”).

parole.significato: crossbow (mechanised weapon based on the bow)
parole.testo: From Old Danish arnbyrst, from Old Norse armbrist, arbyst, from Middle Low German armborst, from Medieval Latin arbalista, from Late Latin arcuballista. Compare German Armbrust and Swedish armborst.
From Old Norse basún, basúna, from Middle Low German basūne, from Old French boisine, buisine, from Latin būcina (“hunting horn”).
From Old Norse blik, from Middle Low German blick.
From Early Modern Danish bever, from Old Danish biæver, biauær. Influenced by Old Norse bjórr, Middle Low German bēver. Cognate with German Bieber, Latin fiber.
From Old Norse dikt, from Middle Low German dicht, dichte, from dichten (“to compose a poem”), itself from Latin dictō (“I compose”).
From Old Norse dikta, borrowed from Middle Low German dichten, itself from Latin dictō (“I compose”).

From late Old Norse edik, from Middle Low German etik or Middle Dutch edik, from Proto-West Germanic *atek, metathesized variant of *aket, from Latin acētum. Compare Norwegian Bokmål eddik, Swedish ättika, Faroese edikur, Icelandic edik, West Frisian jittik, Old English æċed, German Essig.
From Old Norse eins, from Middle Low German eines.

parole.significato: lining (covering for the inside of something)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse fóðr, from Middle Low German vōder (“linen, sheath”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“sheath”).
Equivalent to for- + dømme. From Old Danish fordømæ, from late Old Norse fyrirdœma, from Middle Low German vordomen, from Proto-Germanic *fradōmijaną.

parole.significato: used to indicate that 'something' is being brought forward, presented, or directed at someone
parole.testo: Essentially the same word as the adverb/prefix for-. from Old Danish for-, from Old Norse for-, fyrir-, from Middle Low German vor-.
for- + fader, from Old Norse forfaðir, likely from Middle Low German vorvader.
From Old Danish forgifæ, from Old Norse fyrirgefa, after Middle Low German vorgeven, from Proto-Germanic *fragebaną.
From for- + gå. From Old Norse fyrirganga, from Middle Low German vorgan.
From late Old Norse forstanda, after Middle Low German vorstan, from Old Saxon farstandan. Equivalent to for- + stå. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål forstå, Norwegian Nynorsk forstå, Swedish förstå.

parole.significato: fruit (the seed-bearing part of a plant)
parole.testo: From Old Norse fruktr, from Middle Low German vrucht, from Old Saxon fruht. Cognate with German Frucht.
From føre (“to lead”) + -ing, from Old Norse fœring, partly influenced by Middle Low German voringe.
From Old Danish gift, from Old Norse gipt. Largely replaced by gave, from Middle Low German gave. The word still exists in some compound words, e.g. afgift.
Inherited from Old Norse glas(keri), itself borrowed from Middle Low German glas, from Old Saxon glas.

From Old Danish gryp, from Old Norse gripr (“vulture, griffin”) and Middle Low German grip, via Latin gryps, Derived from Ancient Greek γρύψ (grúps). Doublet of grif and kerub. Compare Old Irish gríb (“gyrfalcon, griffin”).
From late Old Norse hala, from Middle Low German halen, from Old Saxon halon (“to get, fetch”).

From Old Danish hanzkæ, from Old Norse hanzki, from Middle Low German hantsche, colloquial form of hantscho (“glove, gauntlet”), from Old Saxon handsko (“gauntlet, glove”) from hand (“hand”) and skōh (“shoe”) << Proto-West Germanic *skōh.
From late Old Norse heiðneskr, after Middle Low German heidensch. Equivalent to heden (“heathen (archaic)”) + -sk.
From Old Norse heimiligr, from Middle Low German heimelik, from Old Saxon *hēmlīk, from Proto-West Germanic *haimalīk.
Compound of hus + frue, from Old Danish husfrugh, from Old Norse húsfrú, from Middle Low German husvruwe.

parole.significato: hope (belief that something hoped for can happen)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hoop, from late Old Norse hop, from Middle Low German hope.
From late Old Norse kabill, from Middle Low German kabel, from Latin capulum.

parole.significato: candle (light source consisting of a wick embedded in a solid, flammable substance such as wax, tallow, or paraffin)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kerti, from Middle Low German kerte.

parole.significato: to tilt or swing (about a horizontal axis)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kippa (“to snatch”), from Middle Low German kippen. Compare German kippen and Icelandic kippa.

From Old Norse klokka, from Middle Low German klocke, from Medieval Latin clocca, probably of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”) (compare Welsh cloch, Irish clog), from Proto-Indo-European *klēg-, *klōg- (onomatopoeia).

parole.significato: A cup; A concave vessel for holding liquid, generally adorned with either a handle or a stem (confer goblet, glass.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse koppr, from Middle Low German kop, from Latin cuppa.

parole.significato: food (any substance consumed by living organisms to sustain life)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kostr, from Middle Low German kost, koste, German Kosten, borrowed from Medieval Latin costa, which is derived from the verb constare.

parole.significato: to cost; to have a price; to be for sale
parole.testo: From Old Norse kosta, from Middle Low German kosten, from Latin cōnstāre.
From Old Norse kram, from Middle Low German kräm (“fine cloth; also used for merchant tents, thus later a synonym for merchandise”), probably ultimately of Slavic origin; see German Kram.

From late Old Norse kranz, from Middle Low German kranz, from Middle High German kranz, from Old High German kranz, probably altered from krenz, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *kringaz (“circle, ring”).
From late Old Norse kragi, from Middle Low German krage, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷer- (“to devour”).

From late Old Norse krús, maybe from Middle Low German krūs, krōs, of uncertain ultimate origin, but Pokorny proposes an ultimate derivation from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend”), similar to Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“something bent, crooked”), *krukjō (“staff”).
From Old Norse kvik(k)r or borrowed from Middle Low German quik, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz (“alive”). Doublet of kæk and kvæg.
From Old Norse kvittr, from Middle Low German quit, from Medieval Latin quitus, quittus, from Latin quiētus (“quiet, calm”).

parole.significato: candle (light source consisting of a wick embedded in a solid, flammable substance such as wax, tallow, or paraffin)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kerti, from Middle Low German kerte.

From Old Danish køpslaghæ, from Old Norse kaupslaga, from Middle Low German kopslagen (“to settle a deal by shaking hands”). Derived from the noun kopslach. Cognates include Swedish köpslå and Norwegian Bokmål kjøpslå.
From Old Norse lampi, from Middle Low German lampe, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “torch”).

From Old Norse lík (“leech”), borrowed from Middle Low German līk, from Proto-Germanic *līką (“bolt-rope”), cognate with Dutch lijk and English leech. The noun belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *leyǵ- (“to bind”), compare Latin ligō (“to tie”).
Inherited from Old Danish lindorm, from Old Norse linnormr, from Middle Low German lintwurm, from Proto-Germanic *linþawurmiz.

From late Old Norse lykka, lukka, from Middle Low German (ge)lucke, from Proto-Germanic *galukją. Cognate with German Glück (“luck”), Dutch geluk, English luck. Possibly derived from the verb *lūkaną (“to close”).
From Old Norse leikr, from Middle Low German lek, from Latin lāicus (“lay, layman”), from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós, “of the people”), from λαός (laós, “people”).
From Old Danish maklæk, from Old Norse makligr, from Middle Low German makelik. Related to mag.
From Old Danish mæster, from Old Norse meistari, from Middle Low German meister, mēster, from Old Saxon mēstar, from Old French maistre, from Latin magister.
Via Old Norse mǫr and/or Middle Low German mōr, from Proto-Germanic *mōraz.
From late Old Norse mǫguligr, from Middle Low German mogelik. Cognate to German möglich.
From Old Norse murra, likely from Middle Low German murren. Cognate with Swedish morra.
From Old Danish myntæ, mintæ, from Old Norse minta, from Middle Low German minte, münte, from Old Saxon minta, from Proto-West Germanic *mintā, from Latin menta, mentha (“mint”).
From Old Norse máti, borrowed from Middle Low German mâte, mât, from Old Saxon *māta, from Proto-West Germanic *mātu, from Proto-Germanic *mētō (“measure”).
From late Old Norse mektugr, from Middle Low German mechtich, from Old Saxon mahtig. Related to magt (“might, power”). Compare also Norwegian mektig and Swedish mäktig.

From Old Danish møllæ, myllæ, mylnæ, from Old Norse mylna, from Middle Low German molne or Old English mylen, both from Late Latin molina (“millstone”). Related to the verb mylja (“to crush into pieces”).
From Old Norse nauðigr, nauðugr, formed from nauð (“need”), probably influenced by Middle Low German nodech.
From late Old Norse orlof, from Middle Low German orlof. Compare German Urlaub.
From late Old Norse pakki, from Middle Low German packe, from Old Saxon *pakko, from Proto-West Germanic *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.
From late Old Norse pilz, via Middle Low German pels, from Medieval Latin pellicea, from Latin pellis (“skin”).
From late Old Norse perla, from Middle Low German perle, from Old Saxon perula, from Medieval Latin perla.
From Old Norse plata, from Middle Low German plate, from Latin plata, platea, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús).
From late Old Norse planta, from Middle Low German planten, from Latin plantare.
From Old Norse plástr, borrowed from Middle Low German plaster, plāster, from Old Saxon plāstar, from Proto-West Germanic *plastr.

parole.significato: use to, used to (signifies habitual or repeated events or circumstances.)
parole.testo: From Old Danish plæghæ, from Old Norse plaga, from Middle Low German plegen, from Old Saxon plegan, from Proto-West Germanic *plehan. Related to pligt.
From late Old Norse pottr, from Middle Low German pot.
From Old Norse príss, from Middle Low German pris, from Old French pris, from Latin pretium (“price, reward”).
From Old Danish rættæræ, from Old Norse réttari, partly from Middle Low German richter.
From late Old Norse rím, from Middle Low German rim, from French rime (“rhyme”).
From late Old Norse rís, from Middle Low German rīs, from Old French ris, from Italian riso, from Latin oryza, from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza).
From Old Norse rist, from Middle Low German rōsten, from Old Saxon *rōstian, from Proto-West Germanic *raustijan.

parole.significato: rose (flower, shrub of the genus Rosa)
parole.testo: From late Old Norse rós, rósa, from Middle Low German rōse, from Latin rosa (“rose”).

parole.significato: rue (various perennial shrubs of the genus Ruta)
parole.testo: From late Old Norse rúta, from Middle Low German rūde, from Latin rūta (“rue”).
From Old Norse skálkr, from Middle Low German schalk.
From Old Danish skamæl, from late Old Norse skemill, from Middle Low German schâmel, from Proto-West Germanic *skamil, from Latin scamellum, scabellum.
From Old Norse skóli, from Middle Low German schole, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
sko (“shoe”) + -mager (“maker”), from Old Norse skómakari, from Middle Low German schomaker.
From Old Norse skrín, from Middle Low German schrīn or Old English scrīn, ultimately from Latin scrīnium.

parole.significato: tailor (person who makes, repairs, or alters clothing as profession)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skreddari, skraddari, from Middle Low German schrader, schroder.
From late Old Norse speja, spæja, from Middle Low German speien. Influenced by Dutch spieden. Compare Swedish speja, Norwegian speide.

Merger of Old Norse stilla (“to calm”), borrowed from Middle Low German stillen, from Old Saxon *stillian, from Proto-West Germanic *stillijan, and Middle Low German stellen (“to place”), from Old Saxon stellian, from Proto-West Germanic *stalljan.
From late Old Norse stoltr, from Middle Low German stolt, from Proto-Germanic *stultaz. Doublet of stovt.
From Old Norse stoppa, borrowed Middle Low German stoppen, from Old Saxon *stoppon, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn.
From Old Norse stofa, stufa, borrowed from Middle Low German stōve, stūve, Old Saxon *stova, *stuva, from Proto-West Germanic *stobu.
From Old Danish stæfnæ, from Old Norse stefna, perhaps from Middle Low German stevene.

parole.significato: boot (a shoe covering part of the leg)
parole.testo: From Middle Danish støflæ, plural of støfæl, from Old Norse styfill, from Middle Low German stevel, from Italian stivale, from Medieval Latin aestivale. Compare Swedish stövel, Norwegian støvel.

parole.significato: sole (bottom of a shoe or boot, bottom of the foot)
parole.testo: From Old Norse sóli, from Middle Low German sole, from Latin sola, a plural form of solum (“ground, soil”).
By surface analysis, tak + nem + -lig. From late Old Norse þakknæmiligr, perhaps from Middle Low German danknamelik.

Equivalent to tid (“time”) + -lig. Partly from Old Norse tíðligr (“worldly”), tíðliga (“frequently”) and partly borrowed from Middle Low German tīdelīk, tīdeliken (“on time”). Compare also English tidely and German zeitlich

From later Old Norse tilfelli, from Middle Low German toval, itself ultimately a calque of Latin accidens, possibly via Middle High German intermediary zuoval. Cognate with Swedish tillfälle, Norwegian Bokmål tilfelle, Norwegian Nynorsk tilfelle, Icelandic tilfelli. Compare German Zufall (“chance, c

From Old Norse tulkr, from Middle Low German tolk, from Old East Slavic тълкъ (tŭlkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ. This word has also been borrowed to Icelandic túlkur, Norwegian tolk, Swedish tolk, and Dutch tolk.

parole.significato: to chastise; to punish, chastise; to subject to (strict) upbringing or discipline
parole.testo: tugt + -e. From late Old Norse tykta, from Middle Low German tuchten. Compare Swedish tukta and Norwegian tukte.
From late Old Norse turn, from Middle Low German torn, from Latin turris.
From late Old Norse tæra, from Middle Low German teren. Compare Norwegian, Icelandic tæra and Swedish tära.
From Old Danish tynnæ, from Old Norse tunna or Middle Low German tunne.
From late Old Norse úhyrligr, from Middle Low German unhurlich, ungehurlich. Compare German ungeheuerlich. Derived from uhyre (“monster”) + -lig / ungeheuer (“monster”) + -lich.
u- (“un-”) + lykke (“luck”). From Old Danish ulykkæ, from Old Norse úlykka, from Middle Low German ungelucke.
under (“wonder”) + -lig, from Old Danish undærlic, from Old Norse undarligr (“strange”) and Middle Low German wunderlik. Compare German wunderlich, Dutch wonderlijk, English wonderly.

parole.significato: to throw, toss (e.g. fire someone from a job).
parole.testo: From Old Norse varpa. Second definition is from Middle Low German warpen.

From Old Danish weghnæ, from Old Norse vegna, originally a genitive plural of vegr (“way”). The modern construction på vegne af nogen or på nogens vegne "on behalf of somebody" is influenced by Middle Low German van ēnes wegene, cf. German wegen (“because of”), originally a dative plural of way. The
Equivalent to vilje (“will”) + -ig (adjective suffix), from Old Norse viljugr or a calque of Middle Low German willich. Compare also Norwegian, Swedish villig, German willig.
From Old Norse veski, from Middle Low German veske. Compare Icelandic veski, Swedish väska and Norwegian veske.
From Old Danish æræ, from Old Norse æra, from Middle Low German ēre, from Old Saxon ēra, from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀu, from Proto-Germanic *aizō.
